title: The Error of Angel Worship and Legalism
english: Much of this letter is hard to understand, because many people do not know what occasioned it or what the apostle was aiming at. The occasion was this. Believers who had come from among the Greeks had Greeks who were still pagans pulling them back to Greek observances. Believers from among the Jews had Jews urging them to keep the law, as though grace without the law were less than complete. The Greeks’ argument to them was that it is right to worship angels as well, for they said their gods were angels: God is great and out of human reach, and so he supplies his workings to those in need through these angels, as through go-betweens. And the Scriptures too, they said, know how angels help us: God “set the bounds of the nations according to the number of the angels of God” (Deuteronomy 32:8); Michael is the ruler of the Jews (Daniel 10:21); the ruler of Persia is another angel (Daniel 10:13); and again, “Behold, the ruler of the Greeks is coming” (Daniel 10:20). Jacob says, “the angel who delivers me” (Genesis 48:16). In the Acts, about the apostle Peter, they say, “It is his angel” (Acts 12:15). And the Lord said about the children, “Do not stop them from coming to me” (Matthew 19:14), “for their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:10). From all these texts Jews and Greeks alike, some of them believers and some not, drew their conclusion: the grace that comes through the Lord Jesus is superfluous, since the angels, who have been there from the beginning, are enough to bring to God those who obey; and to neglect all the observances kept by Jews and Greeks, they said, was to fall short of perfection. The apostles’ aim in the letter before us is directed against all this.

The second catena form adds: It is worth setting out the occasion of the letter as we have found it from the letter itself. … God is uncontainable … The Jews argued that God set the bounds of the nations according to the number of the angels of God; that Michael is ruler of the Jews; that “the ruler of Persia withstood me” (Daniel 10:13); and “the angel who delivers me from my youth” … And the Lord said, “See that you do not despise one of these little ones, for their angels see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:10). … This is what Paul is aiming at, and he sets these things right. On Colossians 1:2: Notice that in a few lines he names Christ many times. Christ was the one they were setting aside, so Paul keeps mentioning him, to stamp on their souls a longing for him.

On Colossians 1:5–6: He is already showing them that the hope laid up for us, the hope of the resurrection and of the kingdom, was not won by the administration of angels but by the coming of our Saviour Jesus Christ.
